item.title: Trotterized hybrid qubit-boson simulation of the Jaynes-Cummings-Hubbard model
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Trotterized Bosonic Qiskit simulation of a single polariton on an 8-site Jaynes–Cummings–Hubbard chain tracks exact diagonalization with site occupation errors bounded between 10−4 and 10−2, peaking at 6.98×10−3.

Grade 0.477 · 2.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “photonic qubits, linear-optical computing and boson sampling” · Nabaraj Khatri, Dilip Ojha, Rajib Tripathi, Kismat K. C, Ashish Khanal

Figure

Absolute occupation discrepancy |⟨ni⟩Trotter−⟨ni⟩Exact| versus time across 8 individual sites for a single initial polariton, showing saturation within 10−4 to 10−2.

Asks

Can Bosonic Qiskit with a Matrix Product State backend accurately capture many-body real-time dynamics in a Jaynes–Cummings–Hubbard lattice when benchmarked against exact diagonalization?

But

One-dimensional open chains with Fock cutoff d=2 (hard-core photon limit), first-order Trotter decomposition with time step Δt=0.05, and restricted to low excitation numbers (1 or 2).

Tools

Bosonic Qiskit · Matrix Product State (MPS) backend · Trotterized circuit decomposition · Exact diagonalization benchmark

Abstract

The Jaynes-Cummings-Hubbard (JCH) model describes the interaction of light and matter in coupled optical cavities and provides a framework for studying their quantum dynamics. In this work, we design a Trotterized quantum circuit to investigate the real-time dynamics of the JCH model using Bosonic Qiskit and a Matrix Product State (MPS) backend. We simulate single-polariton transport and benchmark site occupations against exact diagonalization results. We then extend the simulations to the two-excitation sector under a hard-core photon constraint, examining excitation transport and symmetry properties. Finally, we study the dependence of bipartite entanglement entropy on the inter-cavity photon-hopping strength. The results illustrate how hybrid qubit-boson circuits, simulated with matrix product states, can be used to study light-matter lattice dynamics. This work provides a numerical benchmark for extending hybrid simulation approaches to more complex interacting and open light-matter systems.

item.title: Blueprint for DOE Quantum Supercomputing
item.description:
Pay dirt review — Lays out deployment targets for DOE fault-tolerant quantum computing: first-generation deployment in 2028 with at least 100 logical qubits executing 10,000 to 100,000 hard logical operations, scaling into the 2030s to 1,000 to 10,000 logical qubits and 1 to 10 billion hard logical operations.

Grade 0.442 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Demonstration of a small programmable quantum computer with atomic qubits” · Ryan Bennink, Robin Blume-Kohout, Salman Habib, Andrew Landahl, Hai Ah Nam, Laura Schulz, Mallikarjun Shankar, Nicholas Wright

Asks

What roadmap, technical milestones, and facility readiness targets must the US DOE establish to deploy fault-tolerant quantum computing for scientific utility by 2028?

But

Strategy and roadmap document; dependent on commercial hardware reaching error correction thresholds and scaling targets by 2028.

Tools

fault-tolerant quantum computing roadmapping · systems integration planning · logical qubit architectures · HPC-quantum hybrid infrastructure

Abstract

Quantum computing stands at the threshold of a transformative decade, where the field will evolve from small-scale demonstrations toward practical scientific computing at scale. This Blueprint identifies fault-tolerant quantum computers (FTQCs) as a viable, scalable, and broadly applicable path to achieving "quantum scientific utility." It outlines a strategy to prepare the US Department of Energy (DOE) for FTQCs and their integration into the US national scientific computing infrastructure. Its purpose is to identify the steps, milestones, and research directions necessary for DOE to enable initial deployment of FTQCs in 2028 as a scientific tool for the nation and mature this capability into the 2030s. Given recent demonstrations of logical operations on error-corrected logical qubits and the advancement of commercial hardware roadmaps, DOE should begin preparations for large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing deployment for DOE science missions. This Blueprint proposes that DOE focus on (1) deploying first-generation scientifically relevant quantum computers with at least 100 logical qubits and performing at least 10,000 to 100,000 hard logical operations in scientifically relevant calculations; (2) developing essential FTQC programming competencies, system software, and facility readiness; and (3) investing in cutting-edge focused R&D that fosters breakthroughs in scientific applications, algorithms, and logical architectures needed to accelerate the advent of scientific utility. This effort will position DOE to transition to larger systems: production-scale quantum computers that comprise 1,000 to 10,000 logical qubits, perform 1 to 10 billion hard logical operations, and execute scientifically useful computations at scale. The Blueprint calls for transformative R&D and collective action to accelerate the advent of scientific quantum utility and bring it within reach by 2028.

item.title: Coherent meson-baryon conversion in a cold-atom non-Abelian lattice gauge simulator
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Realized non-Abelian lattice gauge dynamics with dynamical matter in a cold-atom quantum simulator, mapping an analog system to a gauge sector of a truncated 1D SU(2) quantum link model and observing coherent meson-to-baryon–antibaryon oscillations.

Grade 0.423 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Tian-Yi Wang, Wei-Yong Zhang, Tie-Jin Zhong, Ming-Gen He, Zhao-Yu Zhou, Hui Sun, Zhen-Sheng Yuan, Jian-Wei Pan

Figure

Coherent real-time dynamics between meson population and baryon–antibaryon pairs near the bare resonance g2=−16m/3, showing anti-correlated population oscillations versus evolution time.

Asks

Can non-Abelian gauge-matter interactions and hadronic dynamics with dynamical matter be engineered and microscopically resolved in an analog cold-atom simulator?

But

Truncated link representation (jmax⁡=1/2) restricted to the non-zero Gauss-charge sector 𝐆ˆℓ2=2, Gˆℓz=1 in a 1D chain of up to 20 sites.

Tools

ultracold ⁸⁷Rb atoms in two hyperfine states · spin-dependent optical superlattice · resonant tunneling via magnetic-field gradient · site- and spin-resolved quantum gas microscopy with transverse Stern–Gerlach separation

Abstract

Quantum chromodynamics (QCD), the non-Abelian gauge theory of quarks and gluons, provides a microscopic description of strongly interacting matter, including hadron structure and dynamics. Real-time dynamics and finite-density properties of these systems remain challenging for conventional Monte Carlo methods because of sign problems. Quantum simulation provides a complementary approach, although circuit depth and noise limit digital implementations and non-Abelian gauge-matter interactions remain difficult to engineer in analog systems. Here we realize a non-Abelian lattice gauge model with dynamical matter in an analog cold-atom simulator and directly observe its hadronic dynamics using site- and spin-resolved quantum gas microscopy. This realization is enabled by harnessing two hyperfine states and site-occupation configurations of 87Rb atoms to jointly encode both matter and gauge fields. We tailor resonant tunneling in a spin-dependent optical superlattice to implement a gauge sector of a truncated one-dimensional SU(2) quantum link model with independently tunable mass and gauge coupling. Leveraging this control, we track the conversion of an initially mesonic state into baryonic or vacuum-like configurations through slow mass ramps. Near resonance, we observe coherent oscillations between mesons and baryon-antibaryon pairs and characterize the conversion efficiency as a function of mass, gauge coupling and net baryon density. Our realization establishes an atomic platform for non-Abelian gauge dynamics, opening a route to microscopic studies of nonequilibrium dynamics in strongly interacting matter.

item.title: Physical Realization of the Luczka Model: Inducing Interaction and Entanglement Between Spins
item.description:
Worth a look theory — The exactly solvable Łuczka pure-dephasing spin-boson model is physically realized by noninteracting spins in a plane perpendicular to a unidirectional, linearly polarized photon flux, yielding an effective all-to-all ferromagnetic Ising interaction parameter rapidly approaching −2∑k|gk|2γ2ωk.

Grade 0.419 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · A. R. Kuzmak

Figure

Evolution of bipartite entanglement negativity 𝒩 versus time for spin counts N=2 to 9 in a super-Ohmic environment (s=3, ωc=10, λ=0.01, β=1). Larger N broadens the time window over which maximal entanglement 𝒩=1/2 is sustained.

Asks

Under what physical conditions can the pure-dephasing spin-environment interaction of the Łuczka model be experimentally implemented?

But

Spins must lie strictly in a plane perpendicular to photon propagation (xi=0) with parallel quantization axes, and all photons must be unidirectional and single-polarization.

Tools

unidirectional polarized photon field · pure-dephasing spin-boson mapping · exact operator disentangling · negativity calculation

Abstract

The Luczka model describes the interaction of spins with a common bosonic environment in the pure-dephasing regime, in which the bosonic modes couple directly to only one spin component. Due to its specific form of interaction, the model is exactly solvable and has been widely used to describe spin decoherence and effective spin-spin interactions mediated by a common bosonic environment. However, to the best of our knowledge, its physical realization and the specific conditions under which such an interaction can be implemented have not yet been addressed. Here, we propose a physical realization of the Luczka spin-environment interaction by coupling the spin system to unidirectionally propagating, polarized electromagnetic radiation. In contrast to the original Luczka model, which allows an arbitrary angular distribution of photon wave vectors, our scheme gives a unidirectional photon flux with retaining a frequency distribution of the photons. As an illustrative application of the proposed realization, we investigate spin-entanglement dynamics for coherent, single-mode thermal, and Ohmic

item.title: Programmable multipartite entanglement analogues
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Realized complete Bell-like and Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger-like state families spanning bipartite to five-partite order in classical electromagnetic fields using a programmable spatiotemporal metasurface.

Grade 0.415 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Long Chen, Qing Chun Yin, Zi Xuan Cai, Zhou He, Zhi Cai Yu, Zhihao Lan, Xiaohan Cui, Jian Wei You, Tie Jun Cui

Asks

Can classical electromagnetic nonseparability be programmed to reconfigure the number and identity of entangled degrees of freedom up to high multipartite orders?

Before

Existing classical nonseparable wave implementations largely fix participating degrees of freedom via static generating architectures; classical five-partite nonseparable states were not previously realized.

But

Classical analogues only; lacks true quantum entanglement, quantum nonlocality, and multi-particle quantum measurement correlations.

Tools

programmable spatiotemporal metasurface · electromagnetic state spaces (polarization, frequency, orbital angular momentum, wavevector direction, envelope modes) · GHZ-like and Bell-like state synthesis

Abstract

Quantum entanglement underpins the quantum information science. Its multipartite forms distribute coherence across several subsystems, but controlling their composition and order is increasingly difficult as more subsystems participate. Classical nonseparable waves provide accessible analogues of these structures, although existing implementations largely fix the participating degrees of freedom through their generating architectures. Here we overcome this constraint by making multipartiteness itself programmable in electromagnetic fields. A spatiotemporal metasurface reconfigures the identity and number of coherently linked state spaces independently across polarization, frequency, orbital angular momentum, wavevector direction, and orthogonal envelope modes. We realize complete Bell-like and Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger-like families from bipartite to five-partite order and exchange constituents at fixed order. To our knowledge, the five-partite state has the highest multipartite order experimentally realized in classical electromagnetic fields. These results establish the distribution of coherence across physical state spaces as a programmable property of classical waves and provide a platform for studying selected structures of multipartite quantum states without invoking quantum entanglement or nonlocality.

item.title: Magnetometry and slow light in PT-symmetric cavity optomechanics
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Operating in the 𝒫𝒯-symmetry-protected phase using optomechanical second-order upper sideband generation yields magnetic field sensing sensitivity at the picotesla level and achieves group delays up to the millisecond scale.

Grade 0.414 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Yuguo Su, Tianshun Tan, Yiying Yan, Hengyan Wang, Elijah Omollo Ayieta, Szabolcs Kelemen, Slobodan Radosevic, JunYan Luo, Yi-Xiao Huang, Xingyu Zhang

Figure

Peak second-order upper sideband efficiency θ2max plotted against magnetic field B across different driving powers and current intensities near the 𝒫𝒯-phase transition.

Asks

Can high-order sideband generation and slow-fast light effects in a 𝒫𝒯-symmetric cavity optomechanical system enhance magnetic field detection sensitivity?

Before

Nanoscale cavity optomechanical devices reached 400 nT experimentally, and theoretical first-order sideband 𝒫𝒯-symmetric schemes achieved 0.01 nT.

But

Semiclassical perturbation theory truncated at second order, neglecting sideband orders n>2. Theoretical model without experimental implementation or thermal noise simulations.

Tools

semiclassical Heisenberg-Langevin equations · perturbation theory · coupled loss-gain optical cavities · electromechanical oscillator

Abstract

The generation of optical higher-order sidebands, which produces new frequencies with regular spectral separation, holds significant promise for applications in optical communication and quantum metrology. We investigate second-order sideband generation and tunable slow-fast light effects in a parity-time (PT)-symmetric cavity optomechanics and propose an enhanced magnetometer scheme. We demonstrate that the PT-symmetric structure, an external magnetic field, and the photon tunneling strength provide powerful and flexible control over both the second-order sideband efficiency, as well as the broadening and switching of slow-fast light propagation. Operating in the PT-symmetry-protected phases, our magnetometer based on the second-order sideband achieves a theoretical sensitivity at the picotesla level, surpassing the performance of previous optomechanical approaches. Our results offer new strategies for magnetic field sensing and optical transmission control, paving the way toward applications in quantum sensing and optical information storage.

item.title: Machine Learning-Based Quantum Error Mitigation for Bound-State Simulations
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Residual learning with exact Frobenius-norm convex projection onto valid density matrices estimates ground-state energy as -0.134 MeV (ideal -0.135 MeV, fidelity 0.999) for a 3-qubit Λ-deuteron model, and -3.014 MeV and -3.045 MeV (fidelities 0.995 and 0.998) for 4-qubit Λ-α potentials.

Grade 0.412 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Sumit Choudhary, Tarunpreet Kaur, Harjeet Kaur, Harpreet Singh

Figure

Ground-state energy in MeV (top) and quantum state fidelity (bottom) versus training-set size N for the 3-qubit system. Proposed ML-QEM (blue) converges stably to the exact energy and unity fidelity, whereas conventional ML-QEM (red) drops below the ground-state energy.

Asks

Can residual learning combined with convex projection to physical density matrices improve machine learning-based quantum error mitigation for hypernuclear ground-state simulations?

Before

Unmitigated hardware estimates deviated substantially, and conventional ML-QEM predicted unphysical energies below exact ground-state values (e.g. -3.822 MeV and -3.739 MeV for 4-qubit potentials).

But

Evaluated on 3-qubit and 4-qubit mapped Hamiltonians; required 1600 VQE-ansatz training states, whereas Haar-random training states failed to recover target ground states.

Tools

Residual ML regression (ridge and RBF kernel ridge) · Frobenius-norm convex projection onto density matrices · IBM Quantum hardware · Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE)

Code. https://zenodo.org/records/23969830

Abstract

Noise in quantum devices remains a major challenge for reliable quantum simulations, making quantum error mitigation an important tool for improving their accuracy. Machine learning-based quantum error mitigation (ML-QEM) provides a useful approach, but its performance depends on the training datasets and may produce reconstructed quantum states that are not physically valid. In this work, we introduce an ML-QEM framework that uses residual learning with convex projection to ensure that reconstructed density matrices satisfy physically valid density matrices. We study the effect of different training datasets and regression models using Haar-random and variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) ansatz states. We compare the proposed approach with conventional ML-QEM, readout error mitigation, and zero-noise extrapolation. The method is tested on IBM quantum hardware for three- and four-qubit simulations of the bound Λ-deuteron and Λ-α hypernuclear systems, respectively. For the three-qubit system, ridge regression trained on VQE-ansatz states gives a ground-state energy of -0.134 MeV, close to the ideal value of -0.135 MeV, with a state fidelity of 0.999. For four-qubit system, kernel ridge regression gives ground-state energies of -3.014 and -3.045 MeV, with corresponding state fidelities of 0.995 and 0.998. These results show that physically constrained reconstruction, along with the choice of training datasets and regression models, can improve ML-QEM performance for the quantum simulations studied in this work.

item.title: Phase matching of high-order harmonics driven by a combined coherent and bright squeezed vacuum field
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Adding a weak 1600-nm bright squeezed vacuum to an 800-nm coherent pulse induces sub-cycle phase mismatch offsets, splitting optimal phase-matching gas pressures across harmonic sidebands to approximately 25 Torr for H21.5, 32 Torr for H21, and 38 Torr for H20.5.

Grade 0.397 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Yaoshun Sun, Shang Ma, Xintong He, Jiaao Cai, Wentao Wang, Mingxuan Li, Xiangyu Tang, Sizuo Luo

Figure

Synthesized attosecond harmonic pulses plotted against gas pressure without (a) and with (b) the 1600-nm field, showing sub-cycle optimal pressure offsets from the baseline 32 Torr, and calculated pressure offsets across different field parameters in (c).

Asks

What macroscopic propagation and phase-matching mechanisms produce the distinct pressure dependence of odd, even, and half-integer high-harmonic yields driven by a hybrid quantum field?

But

Semiclassical Husimi-Q sampling assumes large squeezing parameter r (bright-field regime); Kr gas medium; single spatial mode for the bright squeezed vacuum field.

Tools

Husimi-Q sampling · 1D-TDSE with Pöschl–Teller potential · GPU-accelerated deep ResMLP surrogate model · macroscopic Maxwell propagation solver

Abstract

High-order harmonic generation (HHG) driven by non-classical light provides new insights into light-matter interactions and paves the way to quantum attosecond spectroscopy. Achieving phase matching is vital for generating bright HHG sources, while it has received comparatively limited attention in quantum-light-driven HHG. In this work, we investigate the phase matching of HHG driven by an intense coherent field combined with a weak bright squeezed vacuum (BSV) field, using a semiclassical ensemble of coherent-field realizations sampled from the Husimi-Q probability distribution. We reveal the physical mechanism behind the distinct pressure dependence of the harmonic yields for odd, even and half-integer sidebands spectral components, as observed in our previous experiment [arXiv:2607.20941]. The simulations and phase-matching model demonstrate that the BSV-induced perturbation of the electron action phase could introduce an additional sub-cycle phase mismatch, such that the amplitude of sub-cycle bursts could be significantly modified by gas pressure after macroscopic propagation, even when the harmonic yield is near the optimum. The resulting amplitude asymmetry of sub-cycle bursts leads to a significant intensity contrast between half-integer sidebands harmonics, manifesting as distinct pressure dependence of their yields. Our findings reveal the phase-matching mechanism in two-color quantum-light-driven HHG, and suggest opportunities for macroscopic control of the non-classical HHG source.
